examples.solution_text:
Write the reciprocal as a negative power, then use the index law for logarithms.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\log_{6}\left(\frac{1}{13}\right)\\&=\log_{6}13^{-1}\\&=-\log_{6}13\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Use the change-of-base rule to evaluate $\log_{16}64$ by changing to base $2$. Give an exact fraction.
examples.solution_text:
Changing to base $2$ makes both logarithms exact.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\log_{16}64\\&=\frac{\log_{2}64}{\log_{2}16}\\&=\frac{6}{4}\\&=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$

examples.derivation: sqrt(5)=5^(1/2), so log_5(sqrt(5))=1/2. Matches Book 2 line 177 and the square-root item in supplied image3.png.
(a) 7 log_6(6)=7×1=7. (b) -4 log_12(1)=-4×0=0. (c) 6 log_5(sqrt(5))=6×(1/2)=3. Uses the coefficient method in Book 2 Foundation Q2 and its standard logarithmic results.
1/13=13^(-1); the logarithm power law gives log_6(1/13)=-log_6(13). Supported by Book 2 lines 103 and 181–182; the candidate correctly treats the argument as a negative power.
1/sqrt(7)=7^(-1/2), so log_7(1/sqrt(7))=-1/2. Matches the reciprocal-square-root task in Book 2 Q6(i), supplied image4.png.

(1/fourth-root(81))^5=(81^(-1/4))^5=81^(-5/4), so its base-81 logarithm is -5/4. Independently, fourth-root(81)=3 and 81=3^4, giving the same result. Matches Book 2 Q6(l), supplied image4.png, with changed values.
Changing to base 2 gives log_16(64)=log_2(64)/log_2(16)=6/4=3/2. Matches Book 2 Mastery Q8, lines 493–505.
